newsitem.title: USA: LIFFE says markets to decide euro bond makeup.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE says markets to decide euro bond makeup.

text.p: Markets will decide the makeup of bond products traded on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange after planned European currency union in 1999, LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth said Thursday.
"The market will obviously decide this," Wigglesworth said in an interview at the Futures Industry Association annual derivatives conference here.

"It's not clear whether the future bond derivatives in euros, should the EMU project go ahead, will have a single bond as the benchmark...or whether the new euro would be more like the municipal bond market in the United States, where because of different credit assessments there are very different yield bases."
European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is set to merge member country currencies into one single euro.

Wigglesworth said LIFFE must decide by 1998 whether it will have one euro-denominated bond future on one benchmark euro cash bond -- likely to be German government euro debt -- or several different euro bond futures on each country's individual cash euro bonds.
The key determinant will be whether yields between existing German Bunds and other European debt have converged sufficiently by the EMU launch date.

"We can see the potential of needing a different bond future for each country's euro-denominated bond," he said. "At this time it's difficult to say how far that might go in addition to having a dominant German benchmark bond future."
LIFFE has already decided to make its short-term interest rate products exchangeable into a single euro short-term product, but the exchange does not have to decide on its bond products until 1998.

Wigglesworth said it would be better for LIFFE if EMU went ahead with countries having successfully met the strict covergence criteria and a strong euro rather than rushing ahead just to meet the 1999 deadline.
"If EMU is to go ahead it is very important that it will work. It would be a disaster if it breaks up after 3-1/2 years," he said.

He said LIFFE has made provisions in its short-term rate products for an EMU collapse. If a country were to drop out or EMU failed, LIFFE would revert to settling the euro interest rate product in the domestic currency.
